newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Lufthansa profit hurt by fuel costs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lufthansa profit hurt by fuel costs.

text.p: Deutsche Lufthansa AG said on Thursday profits for the first nine months of the year were hit by surging fuel costs, adding it expected full-year profits to be at best 10 percent down on 1995.

But the airline, which is facing fierce competition in its domestic market, said benefits from the huge cost-cutting programme launched last year could put it in line for a significant improvement in profits for 1997.
Lufthansa said pre-tax profits for the first three-quarters fell to 434 million marks ($285 million) compared to 506 million in the same period a year ago, slightly below most analyst expectations.

But chief executive Juergen Weber said the airline was determined to pursue the one billion mark cost-saving scheme announced last year to position it against rivals seeking to make in-roads into the German domestic market.

"We know that the German market is particularly attractive and that Lufthansa is particularly affected and challenged as a result," Weber said, adding that the airline planned to reduce its unit costs by 20 percent by the year 2000.
Shares in Frankfurt-listed Lufthansa initially fell after the results but later came back to trade 12 pfennigs higher at 19.87 marks in a firmer overall market.
Lufthansa said fuel expenses jumped 193 million marks, an 18 percent jump over the nine months, with kerosene prices in September reaching their highest level since during the Kuwait crisis in 1991.
It said the rise in costs had been "unavoidable" even with the hedging operations that airlines carry out on fuel markets to offset such price movements.
In the first nine months, Lufthansa airlines carried some 31.3 million passengers, a gain of 1.4 percent, and the carrier said traffic data for the fourth quarter had so far been "favourable".
But finance chief Klaus Schlede added that fourth quarter profits were unlikely to improve upon the 250 million mark pre-tax figure recorded a year-ago.

"We expect in the best case that profits for this year will be 10 percent below those last year, he said, adding that "a significant improvement" in its profits could be expected in 1997 if cost-savings went according to plan.

Profits in the last quarter of this year are however still at risk from a continuing pay dispute with workers which has already led to brief stoppages earlier this month and cost the firm some 10 million marks in lost earnings.
But financial analysts said the results showed the wider picture for the airline was broadly positive.

"The fact that operating profits include 48 million marks less of proceeds from aircraft sales compared to last time puts a more positive shine on the operating business itself," said Juergen Jungenger, an analyst with Frankfurt-based financial research group Independent Research.
A London-based aviation analyst said the prospect for lower costs and a stronger German economy next year meant there was now a "tremendous opportunity" for profits to rise sharply in 1997.

Lufthansa, which is preparing for the start of the last stage of its privatisation due later this year, is under investigation by German cartel authorities over allegations of charging too much on its domestic routes.
But Weber said the airline was becoming more flexible in its pricing and special offers and had also made service improvements that now put it among the most consistently punctual airlines in Europe.
The airline also said results were dragged down by 66 million marks of losses in its cargo business, which was not expected to make a profit until 1998.
Lufthansa blamed the continued overcapacity in the freight sector for an "inadequate price level" for cargo business.
